title: The Most Expensive Argument You'll Ever Win
author: Greg McKeown
summary: Greg McKeown's short 1-Minute Wednesday column argues that people can keep a conflict alive entirely in their own heads. He confesses to winning imagined arguments with flawless rhetoric and notes the satisfaction never lasted. He cites a 2024 study of 243 employees finding that replaying what went wrong, unlike solution-seeking, predicted worse feelings the next day. From his book Effortless he offers the image of hiring a grudge to do a job, then lists what a grudge cannot do. He qualifies that serious hurts and boundaries still deserve attention, distinguishing remembering an offense from being captive to it. The piece ends with a reflective exercise asking what job the grudge was hired to do and whether to take it off the payroll.
points: Replaying an argument mentally feels productive but mostly repeats the same unpleasant experience.
A 2024 study linked ruminating on what went wrong, but not problem-solving, to worse feelings the next day.
A grudge cannot change the past, force an apology or guarantee safety, so its claimed job is unfulfilled.
The real cost of a grudge is paid in attention, energy and enjoyment of unrelated people.
The practical test is to name the job the grudge was hired to do and act on it or release it.
quotes: I used to love having arguments with others in my imagination. It was particularly convenient because I got to write both sides of the conversation.
Except for this inconvenient truth: while it made me feel better in the moment, it never lasted.
People who spent their evenings looking for solutions to problems did not show the same association with negative feelings the following day as people who kept returning to what had gone wrong.
We can devote hours of mental energy to a problem, fully convinced we are working through it, when we may simply be running the same unpleasant experience through our minds again and again.
Our grudge cannot change what happened. It can't make another person apologize. It can't guarantee we'll never be hurt again.
with many everyday offenses, there's a difference between remembering what happened and remaining captive to it.
We pay with our attention, our energy, sometimes even our capacity to enjoy the company of people who had nothing to do with the original offense.
we hire a grudge to make sure someone else doesn't get away with something. Then we end up paying for it ourselves.
context: McKeown admits to rehearsing imagined arguments he always wins, introducing the habit of keeping a conflict alive alone.
He concedes that the satisfaction of winning an imagined argument is short-lived, undercutting the habit's apparent payoff.
The cited study separates problem-solving rumination from replaying what went wrong, and only the latter predicted worse next-day feelings.
McKeown warns that mental effort spent replaying a grievance can feel like progress while simply repeating the same pain.
The hired-grudge metaphor is tested by listing what a grudge cannot actually accomplish, which undermines its claimed protective value.
He qualifies the argument by distinguishing remembering an offense from being held captive by it, so serious hurts are not dismissed.
The passage itemizes the hidden costs of grudges, which spill into attention, energy and unrelated relationships.
The closing irony reframes the grudge as self-punishment, since the holder pays the price meant for the offender.
